population-variation-s1.title: Rice fields during a blast fungus outbreak
population-variation-s1.text: In a year when rice blast fungus spread through a farming region, researchers compared three kinds of fields. Some fields grew only variety H, a high-value variety the local strain of the fungus can infect. Some grew only variety R, which carries an allele that resists the local strain. Mixed fields grew one row of H for every four rows of R. Twelve fields of each kind were scored at harvest.

table.caption: Infection and yield by kind of planting (means of 12 fields)

population-variation-s2.title: A small, isolated wild cat population before and after new arrivals
population-variation-s2.text: Roads, farms and towns cut a population of wild cats off from all others. By the early 1990s about 26 adults remained. In 1995, eight females from a larger population of the same species in another region were released into the area, and many bred there. Researchers tested cats for genetic variation and examined kittens for inherited defects.

table.caption: Population size, genetic variation and inherited defects
cols: Heterozygosity (share of tested genes with two different alleles)

population-variation-s3.title: Survival by hemoglobin genotype in two regions
population-variation-s3.text: The graph shows modeled survival to adulthood, without modern medical care, for children of three hemoglobin genotypes in a region where malaria is common and in a region where it is rare. The values are based on field studies and rounded. HbA is the normal allele; HbS is the sickle-cell allele.

items.q: Which statement best describes the infection data?
options: Variety H was infected far less often among rows of R than when grown alone
Variety R was infected more often when grown with variety H than when grown alone
Variety H was infected about as often in mixed fields as in fields of H alone
Variety R lost its resistance when grown in the same field as variety H

why.correct: Variety H plants were 58% infected when grown alone but 9% in mixed fields. R stayed near 3-4% either way.
options: Correct: 58% alone versus 9% in mixtures.
R was 4% infected alone and 3% in mixtures, about the same.
H infection fell from 58% to 9%, a large drop.
R's infection stayed low in mixed fields, so it kept its resistance.

items.q: By what percent did infection of variety H fall in mixed fields compared with fields of H alone? Give a whole number.

why.correct: (58 − 9) ÷ 58 × 100 = 49 ÷ 58 × 100 = 84.5%, which rounds to 84% (85% also accepted). The drop is in the share of plants infected, not a drop of 49%.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for variety H being infected less in the mixed fields?
options: Spores from infected H plants mostly land on R plants they cannot infect, so spread slows
Variety R plants release a chemical that kills the fungus, which protects the other plants in the field
Variety H plants grown next to variety R take up R's resistance allele through their roots
Mixed fields were planted later in the season, after the outbreak had already ended

why.correct: In a uniform field, every neighbor is a host, so the fungus spreads plant to plant. In the mixture, susceptible plants are spaced apart by resistant ones, so many spores are wasted and the outbreak grows more slowly.
options: Correct: resistant neighbors break the chain of spread.
The stem describes a resistance allele, not a chemical; and R's own infection data do not suggest one.
Alleles are not passed between neighboring plants through their roots.
Nothing in the setup says planting dates differed; the fields were compared in the same outbreak year.

items.q: Using the ± 2 SE values, which conclusion about yield is supported?
options: Mixed fields beat H alone but are not shown to differ from R alone
Mixed fields out-yielded both fields of H alone and fields of R alone
Fields of R alone and fields of H alone are not shown to differ from each other
The three kinds of planting are not shown to differ from one another in yield

why.correct: Intervals: H alone 3.7-4.5; R alone 5.7-6.3; mixed 6.1-6.7. Mixed and H alone do not overlap, so they differ; mixed and R alone overlap, so a difference is not shown.
options: Correct: no overlap with H alone; overlap with R alone.
The mixed (6.1-6.7) and R-alone (5.7-6.3) intervals overlap.
R alone (5.7-6.3) and H alone (3.7-4.5) do not overlap, so they differ.
H alone does not overlap either of the others.

items.q: The next year a new strain of the fungus appears that can infect variety R but not variety H. Predict which planting suffers the greatest loss.
options: Fields of R alone, because every plant is a host for the new strain
Mixed fields, because they contain two varieties the fungus can attack
Fields of H alone, because H was the variety most infected the year before
The three kinds equally, because the new strain spreads by the same kind of spores

why.correct: A field of one genotype has no individuals that resist the new strain, so it can spread through the whole field. Mixed fields keep some H plants the new strain cannot infect, and H-alone fields resist it.
options: Correct: a uniform field of a now-susceptible genotype is the most vulnerable.
The new strain cannot infect H, so mixed fields keep some unaffected plants and spaced-out hosts.
Last year's strain is not this year's; the new strain cannot infect H.
The strain can infect only one of the two varieties, so plantings differ in how many hosts they offer.

items.q: Which statement best describes the changes from 1990-1994 to 2010-2014?
options: Heterozygosity nearly doubled while both kinds of defect became much less common
Heterozygosity fell while the population size and the share of defects both rose
The population grew, but heterozygosity and the share of defects stayed about the same
Defects became less common before any change in heterozygosity occurred

why.correct: Heterozygosity rose from 0.16 to 0.29, heart defects fell from 21% to 4% and kinked tails from 88% to 18%, as the population grew from about 26 to 120 adults.
options: Correct: more variation, fewer defects.
Heterozygosity rose and defects fell.
Both heterozygosity and defects changed a great deal.
Heterozygosity had already risen by 2000-2004, when defects first fell.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the high rate of inherited defects in 1990-1994?
options: In a small, isolated population relatives mate, so more kittens get two copies of a harmful recessive allele
Small populations make new harmful mutations much faster, so their kittens carried many more new mutations
Low heterozygosity means kittens inherited fewer genes, so some body structures could not form
The defects were caused by the roads and farms themselves, through stress on the pregnant females

why.correct: With few mates available, cats were often related, so kittens more often received the same recessive allele from both parents (inbreeding). Recessive defects then appear, and heterozygosity falls.
options: Correct: inbreeding exposes harmful recessive alleles.
Mutation rate per gene does not depend on population size; the issue is how alleles are combined.
Every kitten has the same set of genes; low heterozygosity means fewer different alleles, not fewer genes.
The defects are inherited and fell after new alleles arrived, which stress would not explain.

items.q: A wildlife manager claims that alleles from the released females caused the drop in defects, not better habitat. Which additional data would best test the claim?
options: Defects in same-year kittens with and without ancestry from the released females
The number of kittens born each year, compared with the number of adult females in the area
Defect rates in the larger population that the released females came from, measured in 1990-1994
The size of the area the population lived in during each period, measured from maps

why.correct: Kittens born in the same years share the same habitat. If those descended from the released females have fewer defects than those that do not, the difference can be traced to the new alleles rather than to conditions.
options: Correct: same years and place, different ancestry.
Birth numbers say nothing about which kittens have defects or why.
This describes the source population, not whether its alleles caused the change here.
Area alone cannot separate the effect of habitat from the effect of new alleles.

items.q: A new virus that kills wild cats reaches the area. Predict how the population would have fared if the virus had arrived in 1990-1994 instead of 2010-2014.
options: Worse in 1990-1994: fewer, more similar cats made resistance alleles less likely
Better in 1990-1994: with fewer cats, the virus would have had fewer hosts and would have died out
The same in both periods, because a new virus is equally deadly to cats of any genotype
Better in 1990-1994, because inbred cats have stronger immune systems from mating with relatives

why.correct: Surviving a new disease depends on some individuals carrying alleles that resist it. A small population with low heterozygosity has fewer different alleles, so the chance that some cats resist is lower, and one outbreak could wipe it out.
options: Correct: low variation makes a population vulnerable.
A small population can still pass a virus among its members, and losing cats matters more when there are few.
Cats differ genetically in how they respond to infection; that variation is what the period comparison is about.
Inbreeding lowers variation, including in immune genes; it does not strengthen immunity.

items.q: In which region do HbA HbS children survive better than HbA HbA children?
options: Where malaria is common, but not where malaria is rare
Where malaria is rare, but not where malaria is common
In both regions, by about the same amount
In neither region; HbA HbA survives best in both

why.correct: Where malaria is common, survival is 92% for HbA HbS and 80% for HbA HbA. Where it is rare, both are 97%: the carrier advantage depends on malaria.
options: Correct: 92% versus 80% with malaria, 97% versus 97% without.
Where malaria is rare, the two genotypes survive equally (97%).
The advantage exists only where malaria is common.
Carriers survive better than HbA HbA where malaria is common.

items.q: HbS HbS children rarely survive to adulthood, yet the HbS allele stays common where malaria is common. Which explanation fits the graph?
options: Carriers, who hold most HbS alleles, survive better than either homozygote, so both alleles stay
New HbS mutations arise each generation fast enough to replace the alleles lost in HbS HbS children
Malaria causes the HbA allele to change into the HbS allele in people who are infected
The HbS allele is dominant, so it spreads whether or not it helps the people who carry it

why.correct: Heterozygote advantage: selection removes HbS in HbS HbS children and HbA through malaria deaths of HbA HbA children. Carriers, with the highest survival, pass on both alleles, so both persist (balancing selection).
options: Correct: the heterozygote has the highest fitness where malaria is common.
New mutations to HbS are far too rare to keep the allele at such high frequencies.
Infections do not change a person's alleles; mutations are random.
Dominance does not make an allele spread; in fact the disease is recessive.

items.q: In a population where malaria is common, the frequency of the HbS allele is 0.10. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg proportions among newborns, what percent of newborns are HbA HbS carriers? Give a whole number.

why.correct: q = 0.10, so p = 0.90. Carriers: 2pq = 2 × 0.90 × 0.10 = 0.18, or 18%. HbS HbS newborns: q² = 0.01, 1%. So about 18 times as many HbS alleles are in carriers as in affected children.

items.q: Malaria is wiped out in the first region and does not return for many generations. No modern medical care is available. Predict the change in each quantity over those generations.

variables.name: Frequency of the HbS allele
variables.why: Without malaria, carriers no longer survive better than HbA HbA, while HbS HbS children still rarely survive, so selection now removes HbS.

variables.name: Survival of HbA HbA children
variables.why: Their main extra risk, malaria, is gone, so their survival rises toward the 97% of the malaria-rare region.

variables.name: Rate at which new HbS mutations arise
variables.why: Mutation is random and does not depend on whether malaria is present.

variables.name: Survival of HbS HbS children
variables.why: Without medical care, sickle cell disease is just as severe; the graph shows similar low survival (18% and 22%) in both regions.

why.correct: The HbS allele was kept common by malaria. Without it the carrier advantage disappears, so the allele slowly declines, while mutation rate and the severity of the disease itself do not change.

items.q: Nearly every export banana is a Cavendish, grown from cuttings of a few original plants. A fungal disease that kills Cavendish plants has spread to many countries. Why is the crop so vulnerable?
options: The plants are clones, so a strain that can infect one plant can infect nearly all of them
Bananas grown from cuttings mutate faster than bananas grown from seed, so they lose resistance quickly
Fungi infect plants grown from cuttings more easily than plants of any kind grown from seed
The Cavendish was bred for flavor, and flavor genes make plants more attractive to fungi

why.correct: Plants grown from cuttings are genetically identical. With no variation, there are no plants carrying resistance alleles to survive, so one pathogen strain threatens the whole crop. An earlier variety, the Gros Michel, was lost the same way in the 1950s.
options: Correct: a monoculture of clones has no variation for resistance.
Propagating by cuttings does not raise the mutation rate; it prevents new combinations of alleles.
The problem is that the plants are identical, not that they came from cuttings as such.
Nothing links flavor genes to fungal infection; the risk comes from uniformity.

items.q: In the 1840s, most potatoes grown in Ireland belonged to a single variety, propagated from pieces of tubers. When a water mold that rots potatoes arrived, most of the crop was destroyed for several years. Which evidence would best support the claim that low genetic variation, rather than bad weather alone, caused the scale of the loss?
options: In the same years, regions growing several varieties lost a much smaller share of their crops
The summers of those years were cooler and wetter than average, which favors the spread of the water mold
Potatoes from the single variety gave high yields in the years before the water mold arrived
The water mold had been reported in the Americas a few years before it reached Ireland

why.correct: If plantings with more varieties suffered less under the same weather and the same pathogen, then variation among plants, not weather alone, made the difference.
options: Correct: a comparison that holds weather and pathogen constant while varying genetic variety.
Wet weather explains why the mold spread, not why one variety was hit so uniformly.
High earlier yields are why one variety was grown; they do not show why the loss was so large.
Where the mold came from does not show why the losses were so complete.

items.q: About 1% of people of northern European ancestry carry two copies of an allele, CCR5-Δ32, that removes a receptor most HIV strains use to enter cells, and they resist infection by those strains. What does this show about variation in populations?
options: Variation already present can include alleles that let some people survive a new disease
HIV caused the CCR5-Δ32 allele to arise in people who were exposed to the virus
A population needs no variation, because one resistant person can protect everyone else
Variation matters for crops but not for human populations, which rely on medicine

why.correct: The allele existed in Europe long before HIV reached people there. Variation already in a population can, by chance, include disease resistance to a pathogen it has never met, which is why genetic variation helps populations survive new threats.
options: Correct: existing variation can contain resistance to new threats.
The allele is far older than the HIV epidemic; mutations are not caused by need.
Resistance protects the person who carries it; a population with more variation is more likely to have survivors.
Genetic variation affects survival of new diseases in any population, human or not.

items.q: Select the two populations most vulnerable to being wiped out by a new disease.
options: A field of potato plants grown from tubers of one plant
A herd of 40 cattle descended from 4 founders, closely inbred for generations
A large wild population of field mice that breeds with nearby populations
A wild grass population of 100,000 plants pollinated by wind across a wide area
A sexually reproducing population of 50,000 frogs in a large wetland

why.correct: Vulnerability comes from low genetic variation: clones and small, inbred populations have few different alleles, so they are unlikely to include individuals that resist a new disease.
options: Genetically identical clones: one susceptible genotype.
Small and inbred: few alleles to draw on.
Large and exchanging genes with other populations: high variation.
Large, outcrossing and widespread: high variation.
Large and sexually reproducing: high variation.

items.q: A small fish of the Atlantic coast carries two common alleles of a gene for the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase. One allele's enzyme works faster in cold water; it is most frequent in the north and rare in the south. How does this variation help the species?
options: Each allele's enzyme works best at a different temperature, so each region's fish suit local water
Fish in the north switch to the cold-water allele when the water cools in winter
The cold-water allele is dominant, so it spreads into the southern populations over time
Having two alleles lets each fish make twice as much enzyme as a fish with one allele

why.correct: Variation in molecules means each population can carry the forms of an enzyme that work best where it lives, and the species as a whole can shift as temperatures change.
options: Correct: molecular variation matched to local conditions.
A fish cannot change the alleles it inherited; frequencies differ between populations.
The allele is common in one region and rare in the other, which dominance alone would not produce.
Heterozygotes make two forms of the enzyme, not necessarily twice the amount.

items.q: Seed banks store seeds of old crop varieties and wild relatives of crops, even ones with low yields. Which reason best justifies this?
options: They keep alleles missing from today's uniform crops, which breeders may need for future threats
Old varieties grow faster than modern ones, so they can replace modern crops when yields fall
Seeds in storage mutate into new varieties, giving breeders a supply of new alleles
Storing many varieties lets farmers plant one variety everywhere, which reduces crop losses

why.correct: Modern crops are often genetically narrow. Old and wild varieties keep alleles, for example for disease resistance or heat tolerance, that can be bred into crops when a new threat appears.
options: Correct: stored variation is insurance against new threats.
Old varieties usually yield less; they are stored for their alleles, not to replace crops.
Seeds in storage are kept dormant and change very little; their value is the alleles they already have.
Planting one variety everywhere is what makes crops vulnerable.

items.q: Which population is most likely to include some individuals able to survive a sudden environmental change?
options: A large population with high variation
A small population with low genetic variation
A population of genetically identical clones
A population descended from two founders

why.correct: More genetic variation means more different alleles and combinations, so it is more likely that some individuals happen to carry traits that let them survive the new conditions.
options: Correct: more variation, more chance of survivors.
Few alleles make survivors less likely.
Clones share one genotype, so a change that kills one may kill all.
Two founders carry at most four alleles of each gene.
